newsitem.title: INDIA: Bankers fight shy of mineral-rich Indian state.
newsitem.headline: Bankers fight shy of mineral-rich Indian state.

text.p: The Indian state of Bihar, rich in minerals and agricultural resources, is a potential haven for investment, but corruption and political turmoil are forcing bankers to shun the state, experts say.
"They (bankers) have cold feet when it comes to Bihar," management consultant Rajesh Sinha said of the state which has rich deposits of coal, iron, copper, manganese and other minerals.

The eastern state, the country's second most populous, accounts for 40 percent of the nation's mineral wealth but has been wracked by Hindu caste animosities, endemic corruption and red tape which have caused political confusion.

The state is located at the heart of a fertile plain irrigated by the Ganges, but its 93 million citizens are among India's poorest. Bihar's annual per-capita income was 3,816 rupees ($106.9) in 1994/95 (April-March), compared with the national average of 8,281.5 rupees.

Matters came to a head last month when chief minister Laloo Prasad Yadav resigned after a court issued a warrant for his arrest in a $280-million "fodder" scandal involving suspected embezzlement of farm funds. Yadav says he is innocent.

Yadav, a charismatic low-caste leader, named his unschooled wife Rabri Devi as successor while his supporters alleged a bias by upper caste authorities in the trial. Yadav was remanded to judicial custody for two weeks last Wednesday.
State administration has been paralysed by strikes and a lack of political will, businessmen say.
Bihar's banks provide less than one-third of their deposits as loans to industry, Sinha said.
In June 1996, Bihar's aggregate deposits were 166.6 billion rupees, while total credit disbursed was around 50.3 billion rupees, or 30.3 percent of the aggregate.
The comparative ratio for Maharashtra, India's most industrialised state, stood at 76.5 percent and a national average of 59.2 percent.
"Banks as a policy lend very little in Bihar," said Nisheeth Jaiswal, secretary-general of the Bihar Industries Association.
Poor infrastructure and red tape have made matters worse for investors despite low labour costs, Jaiswal said. Daily minimum wages in Bihar are as low as 40 rupees ($1.12) a day, he added.

Jaiswal said Bihar also suffered from a decades-old common freight rate policy, under which India's federal government subsidises transport charges for steel in distant corners of India by marking up prices in Bihar, where nearby iron ore and coal mines make it cheaper to produce.
"It is cheaper to get it in Kanyakumari (India's southernmost tip), than 400 km (250 miles) from here," he said.
The common freight policy is being gradually phased out under India's six-year-old economic reform programme, which experts say will nurse back some cost advantage to Bihar.
India's first steel plant, still the largest private plant in the nation, was built more than a 100 years ago by Tata Iron and Steel Company at Jamshedpur.
Centuries of social discrimination based on birth have made for a fragile social fabric in the state, where economic and administrative decisions are often based on social whims.
"We don't have any problems as entrepreneurs," Jaiswal said. "The problem is in the mental approach (in the state)."

Land ceiling laws, under which India's agricultural tracts were redistributed to poor peasants, have been a failure in Bihar, where people from feudal families still play a major role in all political parties.
This has left behind inequities that encourage political apathy and stifle economic growth, Sinha said. ($1=35.7 rupees)
